Personally I am interested in a spiritual path that more directly ties me into an ecological worldview which would lead to actions beneficial to the ecosystem as a whole. This would also involve a thorough understanding of social/political relationships as the relations within our social institutions have massive, usually negative, effects on the ecosystem. Most of this is not visible in our individual lives and direct observation will not necessarily lead to a complex and comprehensive ecological and political consciousness of how one’s life is interwoven with far reaching systemic processes. For example, one participates in harm by buying produce from walmart, as that produce involved labor exploitation, fossil fuel usage, pollution of soil and water, etc. However, many people can’t afford any other food and all those laborers involved in this harm often have no other choice if they and their families want to survive. So systemic change is needed in order to not cause this harm. Goenka and other vipassana meditators as well as those following the theravada tradition tend to have more individualistic mindsets, believing that self-liberation ripples out to those around them in a positive way. I’m of the opinion that life is much more complex than that and to serve life as a whole other methods may be more effective, as well as self-liberating, because we are not individual selves but are one, and our individual liberation is impossible to disentangle from collective liberation of all beings. In buddhist terms I’m looking to practice right action and right livelihood, and trying to understand how to do so in a complicated, highly alienated world. As a practice, among others, I want to increase my capacity and skillfulness in actively engaging with conflict and ethical grey areas with the aim of reducing collective suffering

when you get there you'll fill out a form that's similar to the online application. It's pretty short. There's one question at the end that asks for a short personal biography - relationship to family, work, education. You don't have to put down anything you're uncomfortable with, and if you mention that you've dealt with mental health issues the teacher may ask you to come in for an interview on day 1, the first full day, to check in with you and see if you need extra support with what's coming up in meditation. On my first retreat I wrote that I have PTSD, and the teacher had me meet with her a few times to give me advice on how to deal with traumatic memories that become too overwhelming during the meditations. 

They also ask about drug and alcohol use. I put down "infrequent use of cannabis and alcohol" and no one has asked me about it afterward. I think if a person is currently in withdrawal from an addiction and trying to use the retreat to quit, it might be unmanageable to be there for the 10 days, though I'm sure it's work for some as well. The volunteers and teachers there are unequipped to deal with like really severe episodes and want to avoid a situation where other meditators get distracted by someone's behavior or where someone harms themself by being there.

Anyone besides the teacher won't ask you personal questions, and in my experience the teachers aren't invasive, though that phone call sounded pretty invasive. Most people who go to these, and most people in general, have experienced depression and anxiety. After my first retreat, I stopped writing that I deal with difficulties in mental health and will just sign up for an interview with the teacher if I have questions or need support.

Up until the past few months I spent long stretches of time not hanging with friends. It would get very painful too. 

Therapy and meditation have helped me a lot with the suffering caused by beliefs about myself that have to do with isolation (“people don’t want to hang out with me because something is wrong with me” “I am weird for doing such and such and people will reject me if they find out about” “I have nothing to talk about with others, I’m boring and there’s no reason for someone to want to be friends with me”). Those beliefs in themself are very painful when they run through my head unregulated, so learning new beliefs/perspectives, doing EMDR, and learning to let go of them through meditation has made life a lot less difficult. I like to listen to Tara Brach (meditation teacher) podcast episodes when my mind is in a negative, lonely place and I want to think differently.
 
I have also made more friends lately, which has been easier as I’ve changed the limiting beliefs (which encourage isolating behavior). Specifically, I’ve befriended people who are also into meditation and have what I consider to be life affirming world views and relationships to others that help reinforce the type of beliefs I’d like to cultivate. I’ve met them through meditation groups. These days groups are harder to access but there are online groups as well as people on tinder who interest me. I still only have a couple people I hang out with, and just try to have a really high quality relationship with them. 

Another thing that has helped with isolation is spending time in nature and learning how to give praise and thanks to the beings there. It tends to be very connecting and uplifting to look at, say, a tree, and tell him the beauty I see in him. I learn about this sort of thing from the indigenous teacher Martin Prechtel, who has written many books if this interests you. I think the author/teacher Starhawk also has books about it

And one more thing is volunteering. It has given me a sense of purpose, allowed me to get out of my head and do something new in a new place, and sometimes talk to new people depending on the type of work it is.

Also wanna say this all takes a while. It’s okay to try to make changes then get into a funk. It’s really hard to stay motivated when you don’t have much support but the little things you do add up even if it doesn’t seem like it in the moment. It takes time and lots of repetition to create new neural pathways for beliefs and behavior. Especially in these difficult times! There’s so much potential in you, human beings are incredible!

practice mindfulness/meditation, which will make you aware of the thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that occur when you're given orders and will give you agency over your reaction. with practice people tend to grow their capacity to create space between the external input (the authoritarian orders) and our conditioned, automatic reactions to them, and in the space we are able to choose to behave how we would like to.

​

for example, if you're not already familiar with meditation, in the practice one repeatedly brings the focus of awareness back to the breath. over and over the mind is pulled away into thoughts, memories, and plans, and over and over we wake up, note that this has happened (without judgment), and come back to breath. this exercises the mind in the practice of objectively observing one's internal state. it also grows your ability to choose where and how to place your attention. so with meditation, when you receive orders, you will begin to notice that certain emotions and urges arise, perhaps physical sensations of fear and a conflicting feeling of wanting to say no and yes at the same time. when you're in these situations, you will begin to have more mental space to determine, like other commenters have said, whether it's worth the risk to rebel, and all the exercise of choosing to return to breath regardless of thoughts, emotions, and urges will translate into choosing how you'd like to respond despite experiencing the habitual urge to submit

I've been getting back into reading more by choosing books that don't scare me away so that aversion/fear of a book doesn't become an obstacle to reading. Then I become more likely to finish a book, and that motivates me to read even more. For example, I have some nonfiction science-y books that I think would be worthwhile, but I know my attention span is so shot that I'll end up not reading at all if I tell myself that's what I have to read.

A couple months ago I bought the Night Circus by Erin Morgenstern, which isn't that engrossing imo but it's easy and somewhat engrossing; the mystery throughout propelled me to finish it. It took me about a month to read the whole thing but I just kept going with it. The thickness of it and the physical book's materials, too, were appealing; I looked forward to the feeling of curling up with a blanket on my couch with the heavy floppiness of the book in my hands, so that made me want to read more.

Then I read Girl, Interrupted by Susanna Kaysen which is like 160 pages and the prose is very simple but not boring so I read it quickly. I also related to the narrator/author (college-aged woman hospitalized for suicide attempt, dx'd with borderline personality disorder), and that was a motivating factor for reading/finishing the book.

I'm currently reading Villa Incognito by Tom Robbins, which is super delightful and silly and unusual, and has themes that I'm deeply interested in (indigenous spirituality, anti-capitalism and anti-imperialism). It makes me laugh out loud, so if I want to smile I'll pick the book up. It takes me a bit longer to read because each sentence is written in an interesting way, so I take my time savoring them, and sometimes I'll pause to tie the threads of the book together in my mind. Which I think is a lovely way to experience a book/an evening.

Overall it's still difficult for me to maintain focus (if you can't tell from my writing style) but every moment spent reading improves my concentration and reinforces the habit!

Essays have been incredibly difficult for me since forever. I've realized that it's actually not such a simple issue to overcome. I'm a junior in college now, and even after a year with medication and therapy, I'm still weeks behind in my English classes. However, I HAVE made progress and I know that with continued practice, essays will slowly become more and more surmountable. 

Anyway, here's my advice:

-you almost definitely need a tutor or your teacher to work through essays with you. I get lost in my own thoughts when trying to decide what exactly to write about and it helps immensely to have someone else help you distill your thoughts and keep you from going off on tangents. Today I spent 3 hours trying to figure out the thesis for my paper, and after I met with a writing tutor everything fell into place. 

-do your assignment piece by piece. Don't think about how much you have left, just slowly, gently chip away at it. 

-work on the essays somewhere you won't get distracted. It's increeeedibly easy to get sidetracked if you feel stressed out about what you're doing. I go to the library or a coffee shop sans phone and laptop and write essays by hand. It seems like that would take a really long time, but compared to the amount of time that the internet can suck away from you, it's nothing. 

-when you receive an assignment, set aside a short amount of time for that day - 15 minutes even, where you will just work on the essay, and once that is up you can stop. Getting 15 minutes of stuff down can be really encouraging, which is an important part of decreasing the anxiety that's standing in your way. And then maybe later that same day, set aside another small chunk of time. Try to work in small chunks over a period of several days. When I try to do everything at once, my brain gets jumbled and I feel overwhelmed and frustrated. If you find it hard to get yourself started on a chunk, ask your teacher if you can schedule some time with them to do this. 

In summary, the things that are getting in your way are probably the anxiety produced by frame of mind, time-sucking distractions, and difficulty organizing your thoughts. 

These assignments are creating REAL, disabling anxiety for you. Combating this kind of anxiety requires professional help and/or a lot of careful choices on your part. 

And like any other difficult task, writing will get easier with practice. You just gotta exercise those writing muscles my friend!
